To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the teachers we studied were teaching character in their vocational English classrooms, and that the character education in their classrooms was not explicitly taught but was instead implied by the curriculum.
the curricula of working class students in vocational English classes are implicitly or explicitly focused on character education, and that this focus is grounded in the Protestant Work Ethic.

the teachers in this study, who were all working class and had attended teacher preparation programs at a public university, were all teaching in working class communities and schools and were all teaching students from working class families, were all teaching students who were assumed to need instruction in character education, and all three of the teachers in this case study, who had attended a public university teacher preparation program, were all teaching working class students who were assumed by the teachers to need instruction in work ethic and other character traits.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the ways in which the curriculum for students from lower social classes is assumed to require the development of character traits that will enable students to overcome their presumed deficiencies and succeed in school and society.
the ways in which teachers are socialized to teach working class students and the ways in which this socialization is connected to the character of students from working class backgrounds.
the ways in which the curriculum for working class students is assumed to be a character curriculum, and how this assumption is enacted in the curriculum for working-class students.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the character curriculum in working class and vocational English classes is an implicit curriculum that is designed to prepare students for the world of work and to teach them the character traits necessary to be successful in the labor force.

this study provides evidence that the character education of working class students is a part of vocational and nonvocational curricula, but that this character education does not address the structural and systemic issues that contribute to the underperformance of students from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds.

the curriculum for working class students is a curriculum of character, but that it is a curriculum of a particular character that is grounded in a particular view of the world, a particular view of students, and a particular view of teachers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

teachers in vocational and nonvocational classes in working class high schools are expected to teach students the character traits of hard work, respect, and perseverance, and to do so in ways that do not explicitly name the character traits that are being taught, or the social class and cultural assumptions that drive the teaching.
the teachers in our study, and the curriculum they taught, represented a wide range of approaches to the character education of their working-class students.

the teachers' curricula for working-class students were designed for the students' social futures as workers, and that the students were expected to learn to work hard, respect authority, and manage their personal qualities in order to become productive members of the working class.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the character education that is implicit in the curriculum for students from working-class homes is often a deficit-based curriculum that is not designed to support the development of their academic identities and that the development of academic identities is a key part of the work that teachers must undertake with their students from working-class families.

teachers need to be aware of the ways in whichthey are implicitly and explicitly teaching students character traits and the ways in which these traits are tied to the social and economic structures in which their students are enmeshed.

the curriculum in vocational English and in nonvocational, working class English classes, is a curriculum of character, with the teachers' instruction in the domain of character focused on the development of students' dispositions for success in the world of work.
